mcq.q: The arithmetic mean of 40, 8, 82, 37, 68, 43, 39, 25 is:
mcq.explain: Mean = sum ÷ number of observations = 342 ÷ 8 = 42.75. A quick check: the sum of deviations from the mean is always zero. The average of the smallest and largest values is the mid-range, not the mean.
mcq.fast: Assumed mean: subtract a round number from each value, average the small deviations, add back.

mcq.q: The arithmetic mean of 20, 78, 12, 90, 78, 7, 11, 32 is:
mcq.explain: Mean = sum ÷ number of observations = 328 ÷ 8 = 41. A quick check: the sum of deviations from the mean is always zero. The average of the smallest and largest values is the mid-range, not the mean.
mcq.fast: Assumed mean: subtract a round number from each value, average the small deviations, add back.

mcq.q: Group A has 28 students with mean marks 54; group B has 40 students with mean marks 48. The combined mean is:
mcq.explain: Combined mean = (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂)/(n₁ + n₂) = (28 × 54 + 40 × 48)/68 = 3432/68 = 50.47. The simple average (51) is right only when both groups are the same size. The combined mean always lies between the two group means.
mcq.fast: Weighted average: the answer lies between the two means, closer to the bigger group.

mcq.q: Group A has 19 students with mean marks 56; group B has 17 students with mean marks 71. The combined mean is:
mcq.explain: Combined mean = (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂)/(n₁ + n₂) = (19 × 56 + 17 × 71)/36 = 2271/36 = 63.08. The simple average (63.5) is right only when both groups are the same size. The combined mean always lies between the two group means.
mcq.fast: Weighted average: the answer lies between the two means, closer to the bigger group.

mcq.q: The mean of 21 observations was found to be 70. Later it was found that one observation 88 was wrongly read as 56. The correct mean is:
mcq.explain: Wrong total = 21 × 70 = 1470. Correct total = 1470 − 56 + 88 = 1502. Correct mean = 1502/21 = 71.52. The number of observations does not change; only the total is corrected.
mcq.fast: Shift the mean by (right − wrong)/n = (88 − 56)/21.

mcq.q: The mean of 37 observations was found to be 21. Later it was found that one observation 97 was wrongly read as 10. The correct mean is:
mcq.explain: Wrong total = 37 × 21 = 777. Correct total = 777 − 10 + 97 = 864. Correct mean = 864/37 = 23.35. The number of observations does not change; only the total is corrected.
mcq.fast: Shift the mean by (right − wrong)/n = (97 − 10)/37.

mcq.q: A student scores 97 in Accounts (weight 2), 76 in Law (weight 2), 45 in Maths (weight 4). The weighted average score is:
mcq.explain: Weighted mean = Σwx/Σw = (2×97 + 2×76 + 4×45)/8 = 526/8 = 65.75. Ignoring the weights gives the simple mean 72.67. Weights show the relative importance of each item, so items with bigger weights pull the average towards themselves.
mcq.topic: AM ≥ GM ≥ HM, weighted averages and choosing an average
mcq.fast: Multiply each score by its weight, add, divide by the total weight.

mcq.q: A student scores 54 in Accounts (weight 4), 76 in Law (weight 1), 55 in Maths (weight 3). The weighted average score is:
mcq.explain: Weighted mean = Σwx/Σw = (4×54 + 1×76 + 3×55)/8 = 457/8 = 57.12. Ignoring the weights gives the simple mean 61.67. Weights show the relative importance of each item, so items with bigger weights pull the average towards themselves.
mcq.topic: AM ≥ GM ≥ HM, weighted averages and choosing an average
mcq.fast: Multiply each score by its weight, add, divide by the total weight.

mcq.explain: Arrange in order: 14, 19, 26, 28, 29, 74, 75, 80, 84, 88, 94. With n = 11 (odd), the median is the 6th value = 74. Taking the middle value without sorting is the usual error. The median is not affected by extreme values, which makes it useful for skewed data such as incomes.
mcq.fast: Sort first; middle position = (n + 1)/2.

mcq.explain: Arrange in order: 14, 46, 47, 58, 59, 64, 65, 77, 80, 90. With n = 10 (even), the median is the average of the 5th and 6th values = (59 + 64)/2 = 61.5. Taking the middle value without sorting is the usual error. The median is not affected by extreme values, which makes it useful for skewed data such as incomes.
mcq.fast: Sort first; middle position = (n + 1)/2.

mcq.q: For the distribution 0–10: 13; 10–20: 12; 20–30: 11; 30–40: 5; 40–50: 8; 50–60: 3, the median is about:
mcq.explain: N = 52, N/2 = 26. Cumulative frequencies reach N/2 in the class 20–30 (c.f. before it = 25, f = 11). Median = l + (N/2 − c.f.)/f × h = 20 + (26 − 25)/11 × 10 = 20.91. Use class boundaries for l when classes are inclusive.
mcq.fast: Find the median class from cumulative frequencies, then interpolate inside it.

mcq.q: For the distribution 0–10: 3; 10–20: 20; 20–30: 9; 30–40: 19; 40–50: 21, the median is about:
mcq.explain: N = 72, N/2 = 36. Cumulative frequencies reach N/2 in the class 30–40 (c.f. before it = 32, f = 19). Median = l + (N/2 − c.f.)/f × h = 30 + (36 − 32)/19 × 10 = 32.11. Use class boundaries for l when classes are inclusive.
mcq.fast: Find the median class from cumulative frequencies, then interpolate inside it.

mcq.q: For the distribution 20–30: 8; 30–40: 24; 40–50: 23; 50–60: 15; 60–70: 19, the median is about:
mcq.explain: N = 89, N/2 = 44.5. Cumulative frequencies reach N/2 in the class 40–50 (c.f. before it = 32, f = 23). Median = l + (N/2 − c.f.)/f × h = 40 + (44.5 − 32)/23 × 10 = 45.43. Use class boundaries for l when classes are inclusive.
mcq.fast: Find the median class from cumulative frequencies, then interpolate inside it.

mcq.explain: The modal class has the highest frequency: 120–140 (f = 25). Mode = l + (f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂) × h = 120 + (25 − 6)/(50 − 6 − 20) × 20 = 135.83. Use class boundaries for l when classes are inclusive.
mcq.fast: Modal class = highest frequency; plug f₀, f₁, f₂ into the formula.

mcq.q: For the distribution 10–30: 10; 30–50: 11; 50–70: 11; 70–90: 25; 90–110: 24, the mode is about:
mcq.explain: The modal class has the highest frequency: 70–90 (f = 25). Mode = l + (f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂) × h = 70 + (25 − 11)/(50 − 11 − 24) × 20 = 88.67. Use class boundaries for l when classes are inclusive.
mcq.fast: Modal class = highest frequency; plug f₀, f₁, f₂ into the formula.

mcq.q: For the distribution 10–30: 16; 30–50: 16; 50–70: 20; 70–90: 25; 90–110: 6, the mode is about:
mcq.explain: The modal class has the highest frequency: 70–90 (f = 25). Mode = l + (f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂) × h = 70 + (25 − 20)/(50 − 20 − 6) × 20 = 74.17. Use class boundaries for l when classes are inclusive.
mcq.fast: Modal class = highest frequency; plug f₀, f₁, f₂ into the formula.

mcq.q: For a moderately skewed distribution, median = 71 and mode = 143. The mean is about:
mcq.explain: Empirical relationship (Karl Pearson): Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean, equivalently Mean − Mode = 3(Mean − Median). With mean 35, median 71 and mode 143: 3 × 71 − 2 × 35 = 143. Solving for the missing value gives 35.
mcq.fast: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean; rearrange for the unknown.

mcq.q: For a moderately skewed distribution, mean = 20 and median = 67. The mode is about:
mcq.explain: Empirical relationship (Karl Pearson): Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean, equivalently Mean − Mode = 3(Mean − Median). With mean 20, median 67 and mode 161: 3 × 67 − 2 × 20 = 161. Solving for the missing value gives 161.
mcq.fast: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean; rearrange for the unknown.

mcq.q: For a moderately skewed distribution, median = 58 and mode = 26. The mean is about:
mcq.explain: Empirical relationship (Karl Pearson): Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean, equivalently Mean − Mode = 3(Mean − Median). With mean 74, median 58 and mode 26: 3 × 58 − 2 × 74 = 26. Solving for the missing value gives 74.
mcq.fast: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean; rearrange for the unknown.

mcq.q: The geometric mean of 4, 16 is:
mcq.explain: GM = (product of the values)^(1/n) = (4 × 16)^(1/2) = 64^(1/2) = 8. It is used for averaging ratios and growth rates. The arithmetic mean 10 is larger, as AM ≥ GM always for positive numbers.
mcq.fast: Write each value as a power of 2; GM = 2^(average power).

mcq.q: The geometric mean of 9, 1 is:
mcq.explain: GM = (product of the values)^(1/n) = (9 × 1)^(1/2) = 9^(1/2) = 3. It is used for averaging ratios and growth rates. The arithmetic mean 5 is larger, as AM ≥ GM always for positive numbers.
mcq.fast: Write each value as a power of 3; GM = 3^(average power).

mcq.q: Towns P and Q are 180 km apart. A car goes from P to Q at 60 km/h and comes back from Q to P at 40 km/h. Its average speed for the round trip is:
mcq.explain: For equal distances, average speed = total distance/total time = 2D/(D/60 + D/40) = 2 × 60 × 40/(60 + 40) = 48 km/h, the harmonic mean. The simple average 50 km/h is wrong because more time is spent at the slower speed.
mcq.fast: Equal distances ⇒ HM = 2ab/(a + b); the distance does not matter.

mcq.q: Towns P and Q are 360 km apart. A car goes from P to Q at 30 km/h and comes back from Q to P at 20 km/h. Its average speed for the round trip is:
mcq.explain: For equal distances, average speed = total distance/total time = 2D/(D/30 + D/20) = 2 × 30 × 20/(30 + 20) = 24 km/h, the harmonic mean. The simple average 25 km/h is wrong because more time is spent at the slower speed.
mcq.fast: Equal distances ⇒ HM = 2ab/(a + b); the distance does not matter.

mcq.explain: Sort: 12, 18, 27, 37, 45, 50, 51, 55, 69, 74, 79, 84, 86, 91, 97. Q1 is at position 1(n + 1)/4 = 1(16)/4 = 4. That is the 4th value, 37. Always sort the data first. Q₁ has a quarter of the observations below it and Q₃ has three quarters below it.
mcq.fast: Sort, find position k(n + 1)/4, interpolate if it is fractional.

mcq.explain: Sort: 26, 31, 33, 37, 41, 49, 58, 59, 62, 66, 67, 73, 74, 94, 95. Q1 is at position 1(n + 1)/4 = 1(16)/4 = 4. That is the 4th value, 37. Always sort the data first. Q₁ has a quarter of the observations below it and Q₃ has three quarters below it.
mcq.fast: Sort, find position k(n + 1)/4, interpolate if it is fractional.

mcq.q: Using the (n + 1) rule, the third quartile of 76, 28, 32, 59, 26, 71, 42, 23, 43, 51, 89, 52 is:
mcq.explain: Sort: 23, 26, 28, 32, 42, 43, 51, 52, 59, 71, 76, 89. Q3 is at position 3(n + 1)/4 = 3(13)/4 = 9.75. Interpolate between the 9th (59) and 10th (71) values: 59 + 0.75 × 12 = 68. Always sort the data first. Q₁ has a quarter of the observations below it and Q₃ has three quarters below it.
mcq.fast: Sort, find position k(n + 1)/4, interpolate if it is fractional.

mcq.q: Two variables are related by 3x − 3y = 6. If the mean of x is 37, the mean of y is:
mcq.explain: Rewrite: y = (6 − 3x)/-3. Averages (mean, median, mode) follow the same linear change of origin and scale, so mean of y = (6 − 3 × 37)/-3 = 35. Keep the sign of -3 when dividing.
mcq.fast: Put the given average of x straight into the equation and solve for y.

mcq.q: Two variables are related by 6x + 2y = 49. If the mean of x is 47, the mean of y is:
mcq.explain: Rewrite: y = (49 − 6x)/2. Averages (mean, median, mode) follow the same linear change of origin and scale, so mean of y = (49 − 6 × 47)/2 = -116.5. Keep the sign of 2 when dividing.
mcq.fast: Put the given average of x straight into the equation and solve for y.

mcq.q: The arithmetic mean of two positive numbers is 18.5 and their geometric mean is 6. The larger number is:
mcq.explain: Sum = 2 × AM = 37 and product = GM² = 36. The numbers are the roots of t² − 37t + 36 = 0, i.e. 1 and 36. The larger number is 36.
mcq.topic: AM ≥ GM ≥ HM, weighted averages and choosing an average
mcq.fast: Find two numbers with sum 37 and product 36 — test the options.

mcq.q: The arithmetic mean of two positive numbers is 22.5 and their geometric mean is 18. Their harmonic mean is:
mcq.explain: For two positive numbers, GM² = AM × HM. So HM = GM²/AM = 324/22.5 = 14.4. This also confirms AM ≥ GM ≥ HM: 22.5 ≥ 18 ≥ 14.4. (The numbers are 9 and 36.)
mcq.topic: AM ≥ GM ≥ HM, weighted averages and choosing an average
mcq.fast: HM = GM² ÷ AM for two numbers.

mcq.q: The mean of the values 39, 38, 27, 52, 45, 8 and x is 34. Then x =
mcq.explain: Total of all 7 values = mean × n = 34 × 7 = 238. The given values add to 209, so x = 238 − 209 = 29. Dividing by 6 instead of 7 forgets that x is itself one of the observations.
mcq.fast: x = mean × (number of values) − sum of the known values.

mcq.q: The mean of the values 20, 46, 22, 36, 20, 35 and x is 30. Then x =
mcq.explain: Total of all 7 values = mean × n = 30 × 7 = 210. The given values add to 179, so x = 210 − 179 = 31. Dividing by 6 instead of 7 forgets that x is itself one of the observations.
mcq.fast: x = mean × (number of values) − sum of the known values.
